title: Cost-Aware Stopping for Freeze–Thaw Bayesian Optimization: When Does One-Step Lookahead Suffice?

paper.title: Cost-Aware Stopping for Freeze–Thaw Bayesian Optimization: When Does One-Step Lookahead Suffice?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Freeze–thaw Bayesian optimization (BO) evaluates candidates in resumable increments but usually stops at a budget or
convergence test. We maximize a budget-free utility, the best observed score minus a cost per increment, with a one-step lookahead:
advance the candidate with the largest expected improvement (EI) under a fixed surrogate, and stop once no EI exceeds the
cost. This rule, EI stopping , never falls below stopping immediately in expected utility, yet it can stop too early. We construct a certificate, a
lower bound on the value of two-step lookahead, that proves such a stop premature, and repeating this correction never lowers
expected utility under the surrogate. Under the surrogate, EI stops are premature on average at low costs and lose little at
high costs. On three hyperparameter optimization benchmarks, a pre-registered test finds EI stopping noninferior to the
correction in most high-cost settings, while the correction gains at low costs on two of the three; more information sharing
in the surrogate raises EI stopping’s utility. On the surrogates of two published methods, EI stopping trades lower scores
for fewer training increments. EI stopping is a simple cost-aware reference whose utility depends on the surrogate.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Freeze–thaw Bayesian optimization (BO) allocates evaluation effort among candidates in resumable increments, allowing any candidate’s evaluation to be paused and resumed ( Swersky et al., 2014 ; Rakotoarison et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2025 ) . In hyperparameter optimization (HPO), candidates are hyperparameter configurations and increments are epochs or checkpoints. The original Freeze–Thaw BO method ( Swersky et al., 2014 ) and later learning-curve models use this to allocate training adaptively ( Wistuba et al., 2022 ; Kadra et al., 2023 ; Rakotoarison et al., 2024 ) , and curve extrapolation also ends unpromising runs early ( Domhan et al., 2015 ; Dai et al., 2019 ; Adriaensen et al., 2023 ) . These searches usually end at a supplied budget ( Swersky et al., 2014 ; Wistuba et al., 2022 ; Rakotoarison et al., 2024 ) , by a regret-based convergence test ( Makarova et al., 2022 ; Ishibashi et al., 2023 ; Wilson, 2024 ) or by a utility-regret threshold ( Lee et al., 2025 ) . We treat allocation and stopping in fixed-pool freeze–thaw BO as one decision problem and maximize the utility y ~ τ − λ ​ τ \tilde{y}_{\tau}-\lambda\tau , the best score observed when the search stops after τ \tau evaluation increments minus a cost λ \lambda per increment (Section 3.1 ). The cost alone governs termination, so no budget or horizon is needed, and maximizing utility minimizes the cost-adjusted simple regret of Xie et al. (2026) with a uniform cost (Appendix G ). We study a simple rule that targets this objective, EI stopping: train the configuration with the largest expected improvement (EI) ( Jones et al., 1998 ) while max i ⁡ EI i > λ \max_{i}\mathrm{EI}_{i}>\lambda and stop otherwise. EI-threshold stopping has been analyzed for its regret ( Nguyen et al., 2017 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) , and for complete evaluations Xie et al. (2026) derive the threshold from the Pandora’s box index ( Weitzman, 1979 ) . The rule looks one step ahead: the Bellman equation splits the value of an advance into its net gain EI i − λ \mathrm{EI}_{i}-\lambda and a nonnegative option value (Equation ( 3 )), and EI stops are Bellman-optimal under forward closure (Theorem 1 ), which learning curves need not satisfy: an unprofitable increment can unlock a later fidelity, or reveal which other configuration deserves training (Appendix A.4 ); the second requires a surrogate that shares information across configurations (Proposition 4 ). We ask whether EI stopping is limited by the depth of its lookahead or by the surrogate. We compare it, exactly under the surrogate and on recorded curves, with H2 stopping , its certified two-step correction, which keeps greedy EI allocation and at an EI stop certifies a candidate advance by its two-step continuation value. Our contributions are as follows. • Theory. We characterize premature EI stops through the Bellman option value and show that a positive lower bound on the value of a feasible two-step lookahead, the gate , proves an EI stop premature under the surrogate. The bound isolates a switching premium that arises only when the surrogate shares information across configurations, and repeating the gate at every EI stop never lowers expected utility, for any finite cap on further training (Section 4 ). EI stopping itself trains for at most 1 / λ 1/\lambda further increments in expectation and never falls below stopping immediately (Lemma 1 ), the freeze–thaw BO counterpart of the guarantee of Xie et al. (2026) . • Certified computation. For Gaussian surrogates with affine fantasy updates, slope-screened endpoint enclosures bound the selected configuration’s H2 advantage with directed rounding ( Fousse et al., 2007 ) (Section 4.3 ). • Controlled empirical study. We build three Gaussian learning-curve surrogates, GP-a, GP-at and GP-atJ, that share asymptotes across configurations and differ only in how they share transients: not at all, through the hyperparameter kernel, or also through a task-wide term; GP-atJ is the primary surrogate (Section 5 ). We cross them with EI stopping and H2 stopping on LCBench ( Zimmer et al., 2021 ) , PD1 ( Wang et al., 2024 ) and the held-out ODBench ( Lee et al., 2025 ) (Section 6 ). Four findings emerge. (F1) Under the surrogate, EI stops are premature on average at low costs and lose little at high costs. (F2) On recorded curves, certified departures gain most at low costs, except on LCBench, and little at high costs, where EI stopping is mostly noninferior. (F3) The pattern holds across all three Gaussian surrogates, and more information sharing significantly raises EI stopping’s average utility. (F4) On the surrogates of ifBO and DyHPO, EI stopping trades lower scores for fewer training increments.

sections.heading: Learning-Curve Models and Sharing.
sections.text: Freeze–Thaw BO couples asymptotes through a GP over hyperparameters, models transients independently, and has no rule for ending the search ( Swersky et al., 2014 ) . DyHPO, DPL, LC-PFN and ifBO/FT-PFN are learned alternatives ( Wistuba et al., 2022 ; Kadra et al., 2023 ; Adriaensen et al., 2023 ; Rakotoarison et al., 2024 ) , and CFBO adds cost-sensitive acquisition, a stopping rule and a transfer-trained extrapolator ( Lee et al., 2025 ) . Our controls are Gaussian processes ( Rasmussen and Williams, 2006 ) that keep the asymptote-plus-transient form of Freeze–Thaw BO’s learning-curve model; they isolate information sharing while keeping fantasies certifiable.

sections.heading: Cost-Aware Stopping.
sections.text: EI-threshold termination has prior treatments ( Nguyen et al., 2017 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . The closest work to our objective is Xie et al. (2026) , who pair a cost-aware stopping rule with PBGI and LogEIPC ( Xie et al., 2024 ) , the log variant ( Ament et al., 2023 ) of EI per unit cost ( Snoek et al., 2012 ) ; under uniform cost, LogEIPC with their rule is EI stopping. Their evaluations are complete, a full 51-epoch run on LCBench, and multi-fidelity evaluation is listed as an extension; we study freeze–thaw BO, where an action is one epoch or checkpoint, and ask what downstream value the EI stopping boundary misses there. Other whole-search criteria use error scales, regret gaps or probabilistic tolerances ( Makarova et al., 2022 ; Ishibashi et al., 2023 ; Wilson, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . These tests are cost-blind: the cost of continuing does not enter them, whereas EI stopping weighs the expected gain of the next increment against its cost. Fixed-schedule methods ( Jamieson and Talwalkar, 2016 ; Li et al., 2018 ; Falkner et al., 2018 ; Li et al., 2020 ) follow a preset schedule. We compare with neither.

sections.heading: Non-Myopic Decisions and Policy Improvement.
sections.text: Forward closure makes one-step stopping optimal in classical monotone problems and on transition-closed sets of metalevel states ( Chow et al., 1971 ; Ferguson, 2008 ; Hay et al., 2012 ) ; Theorem 1 gives the version for our setting. Rollout and policy improvement instead compare actions using a base policy ( Tesauro and Galperin, 1996 ; Bertsekas et al., 1997 ) , and non-myopic BO values future information by simulating the observations it would receive ( Jiang et al., 2020 ; Yue and Al Kontar, 2020 ) . Conservative and safe policy improvement certify gains from sampled data ( Kakade and Langford, 2002 ; Laroche et al., 2019 ) ; ours holds under the surrogate. Martingale duality and information relaxations give dual upper bounds on the optimal value ( Rogers, 2002 ; Haugh and Kogan, 2004 ; Brown et al., 2010 ) ; our certificate gives lower bounds only and thus measures what a correction recovers, and F1 (Section 6.2 ) computes the exact gap on reduced instances. Appendix A.6 relates allocation in freeze–thaw BO to optimal switching and Pandora-type search ( Carmona and Ludkovski, 2008 ; Weitzman, 1979 ) .

sections.heading: 4.3 Analytical Enclosure
sections.text: We compute the certified bound of Algorithm 1 (line 5 ) for the fixed Gaussian planning laws of Section 5 . sections.heading: 6.2 Findings under the Controlled Surrogates
sections.text: F1: EI stops are premature on average at the lower costs. At a fixed EI stop, increasing the cost cannot increase the optimal continuation premium. We compute the gap to the Bellman optimum exactly on small instances: EI stopping episodes under GP-atJ, frozen at their first EI stop and reduced to three arms with two further increments each ( 3 × 2 3{\times}2 instances) or two arms with three ( 2 × 3 2{\times}3 ; Appendix E.1 ). Dropping arms and increments only removes options, so the instances can show that a stop is premature but not that it is optimal in the full problem. On 840 pre-registered 3 × 2 3{\times}2 instances over all seven costs, the EI stop is exactly optimal in 72.5% and within one increment’s cost in 89.8%, and ideal H2 stopping, which uses the exact advantage, recovers 99.2% of the gap (85.5% on 2 × 3 2{\times}3 instances). The gap concentrates at low cost: at the two highest costs the stop is optimal in 84% and 78% of 3 × 2 3{\times}2 and 2 × 3 2{\times}3 instances, and below them in 68% and 54%. (Figure 1 ; Table 4 ). On the full pool, lower and upper bounds on the gap at the same 840 states (Table 5 ) show the EI stop premature on average at every cost up to 0.001 0.001 , and at 0.002 0.002 on PD1 and ODBench. At the two highest costs the lower bound is below one increment’s cost, but the upper bound is too loose to establish any cell near-optimal. F2: On recorded curves, certified departures gain most at low costs and little at high costs, with losses recorded on LCBench. The gate’s effect is nonnegative under the surrogate (Corollary 1 ); on recorded curves it is measured. The gate opens at the first EI stop in 4–29% of episodes at the four highest costs and in 19–43% at the three lower ones. It changes mean utility by less than one increment’s cost at λ ≥ 0.001 \lambda\geq 0.001 , and below that by up to 18 times that cost on PD1 and 11 times on ODBench. The pre-registered test finds EI stopping noninferior to H2 stopping in 10 of 21 cells, seven of the nine at λ ≥ 0.002 \lambda\geq 0.002 . Certified continuation gains significantly in two cells (PD1 at λ = 0.0002 \lambda=0.0002 ; ODBench at λ = 0.0001 \lambda=0.0001 ) and loses in three (LCBench at λ = 0.0005 \lambda=0.0005 , 0.001 0.001 and 0.002 0.002 ). sections.heading: 6.3 Score–Resource Tradeoffs on Published Surrogates
sections.text: F4: EI stopping trades score for fewer training increments, with the exchange valued by utility. We run EI stopping on the surrogates of ifBO and DyHPO, which are FT-PFN and a deep-kernel GP ( Wilson et al., 2016 ) (Table 2 ; Appendix F ). Run to a budget of 300 increments, ifBO and DyHPO return higher mean scores in every cell, using 39 39 to 292 292 more increments on average. EI stopping attains the higher utility when the priced increments it saves exceed the score it gives up: the break-even cost λ ⋆ \lambda^{\star} , mean score loss over mean increments saved, ranges from 0.00002 0.00002 to 0.00038 0.00038 (Table 15 ), and the utility-difference band lies above zero in 20 of 21 cells against each budgeted method, the remaining cells at λ = 0.0001 \lambda=0.0001 . Against CFBO-NT (CFBO without its transfer-trained extrapolator), EI stopping has higher scores and utility-difference bands above zero in all 21 cells.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: The two-step gate certifies EI stops made premature by delayed fidelity gains or by observation-dependent switching. Under the surrogate, EI stops lose value at low costs and little at high costs, while full-scale near-optimality remains open. On recorded curves, EI stopping is noninferior to its certified correction in most high-cost settings; at lower costs the correction gains on PD1 and loses on LCBench under all three surrogates, and more information sharing raises EI stopping’s utility. On published surrogates, EI stopping trades lower scores for fewer increments, which utility prices at each cost. The certificate finds value that one-step stopping misses; experiments on recorded curves test whether it is realized.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our results concern one utility: linear in a cost per increment, risk-neutral, and defined on the best observed score. An increment is a benchmark-defined checkpoint that also fixes the lookahead depth and the surrogate’s timescales, so findings by cost are relative to each benchmark’s unit, and differences between benchmarks are confounded with that unit (Appendix G ). The certificate’s computational cost is not charged in the objective. The experiments replay fixed pools on three HPO benchmarks; at the lowest costs, some configuration’s recorded curve has already run out at up to nine in ten EI stops (Appendix E.5 ). The surrogates are fixed in advance and fitted to no curves; we test neither a fitted planning law nor cost-aware regret-based stopping.

The history state space is standard Borel; F , h λ F,h_{\lambda} and the fixed transition kernel p θ p_{\theta} are measurable; the finite-valued availability correspondence has measurable graph. The cost of b b increments is λ ​ b \lambda b with λ > 0 \lambda>0 , where b b is the global count of increments. Randomized policies are represented by an exogenous seed that, conditional on the current state, is independent of all future potential observation streams. Assumption 1 fixes the rule mapping history to a predictive distribution, including all predetermined updates. A prescribed retraining procedure can define such a kernel; a rollout must then include that procedure at every fantasized history. Our Gaussian implementation fixes hyperparameters so that those updates admit the enclosure of Section 4.3 (Appendix F.4 ). Assumption 2 rules out unbounded scores and rescaling by observed outcomes; the incumbent’s gain is therefore bounded. Assumption 3 rules out free increments; every increment thus has a positive cost, and EI stopping trains finitely often in expectation (Lemma 1 ).

sections.heading: A.6 Search and Switching
sections.text: A freeze–thaw BO policy chooses at each step which arm to advance or whether to stop. Unlike optimal switching between regimes ( Carmona and Ludkovski, 2008 ) , an arm that is not advanced does not evolve, which is the structure of Pandora-type search. The index of Weitzman (1979) assumes independent boxes, each opened in a single stage; a freeze–thaw arm is inspected over many stages and, under a shared surrogate, is correlated with the others. Independent and correlated Pandora models clarify how inspection can direct later search ( Weitzman, 1979 ; Chawla et al., 2023 ) ; posterior BO indices have different updating semantics ( Xie et al., 2024 ) . Multistage and nested Pandora models extend Weitzman’s index to boxes inspected in several stages whose value is claimed only after the last ( Kleinberg et al., 2016 ; Gupta et al., 2019 ; Bowers and Waggoner, 2026 ) , and Markov search processes with costly choices generalize them further ( Bowers et al., 2026 ) . A freeze–thaw arm differs in that every reading counts toward the incumbent, so the search may leave an arm at any stage and keep its best reading, as on the lines of Pandora’s box with order constraints, whose readings are independent ( Boodaghians et al., 2023 ) . Knowledge-gradient policies value the same option term through the expected gain of one more measurement ( Frazier et al., 2008 ) , and their trace-aware multi-fidelity form values continuing a training curve at its cost ( Wu et al., 2020 ) ; both are acquisition rules without a certified stop.

sections.heading: Scope of the Three Claims.
sections.text: The ideal policy comparison concerns the fixed planning law. The numerical certificate verifies the EI boundary and the selected root’s advantage from the exact binary state inputs, after floating-point EI and the point planner choose the EI stopping action and the candidate. Transferring Corollary 1 to the floating-point policy additionally requires all EI stopping actions to agree with exact-arithmetic EI throughout its reachable subtree, beyond the replay path. The empirical comparison asks whether the certified departure is profitable on benchmark curves, which must be tested even when the expectation under the planning law is positive.

sections.heading: D.1 Benchmarks
sections.text: LCBench. All 35 tasks of the data_2k_lw release ( Zimmer et al., 2021 ) , with 2,000 configurations each and one checkpoint per epoch over 50 epochs; the score is validation accuracy. PD1. We use 15 tasks of Wang et al. (2024) and the 242 of 400 configurations with complete, non-diverged phase-1 records on every task. Eight further tasks carry at most six usable checkpoints each, against 12 to 1,413 for the 15 retained, and are excluded because replay caps would dominate the stopping decision there; the exclusion uses only native horizon length and is applied when the benchmark cache is built. The shared intersection gives every comparison the same finite pool but conditions evaluation on configurations that survive on every task. We replay stored scores without interpolation and drop every curve’s final observation, which follows a shorter terminal interval. Of the 15 tasks, 13 use 1,000-optimizer-step spacing between retained checkpoints, LM1B 29,590 and UniRef50 10,000; one checkpoint, and its λ \lambda charge, therefore denotes different amounts of training on different tasks. The three tasks with more than 100 checkpoints, the two ImageNet ResNet workloads and the WMT translation Transformer, have 250 to 1,413; the other 12 tasks have 12 to 52. The four hyperparameter coordinates are transformed and min–max scaled once over the 242-point candidate set. ODBench. The object-detection learning-curve dataset of Lee et al. (2025) , built on datasets from Roboflow 100 ( Ciaglia et al., 2022 ) ; the paper leaves it unnamed, and we use the name of its public release. Each of the release’s 30 tasks pairs a dataset with one of three detectors, Faster R-CNN with a ResNet-50 or HRNet backbone or SSDLite with MobileNetV2, and holds 500 configurations of batch size, learning rate, momentum and weight decay trained for 20 epochs. We use nine tasks, datasets 8–10 with each detector, and their native bounded validation score. Hyperparameter coordinates are normalized from the known candidate values. Under the discretized planning law, each instance’s gap V λ ⋆ − V π EI V_{\lambda}^{\star}-V_{\pi_{\rm EI}} is therefore a lower bound on the gap of the full pool with its full horizons, and the optimal and within- λ \lambda shares are upper bounds on the full pool’s. sections.heading: Full Scale.
sections.text: The reduced instances bound the full pool’s gap from one side only. A second pre-registered study bounds it from both sides at the same 840 states, with all 32 arms and every recorded increment (Table 5 ). A long-lookahead policy π LA \pi_{\rm LA} , which advances the arm for which the expected improvement of its n n -th further score over the incumbent most exceeds n ​ λ n\lambda , over a grid of n n up to the arm’s remaining increments, and runs for at most 300 increments, gives a Monte Carlo lower bound under the planning law (its index uses the Gaussian marginal of the n n -th score, a proxy that affects the policy’s quality but not the validity of the bound); an information relaxation that reveals the component the arms share, with a martingale penalty ( Brown et al., 2010 ) , gives an upper bound. The rebuilt states match the reduced study’s, and on the reduced instances the full-scale code reproduces the exact optimum. At every cost up to 0.001 0.001 , and at 0.002 0.002 on PD1 and ODBench, π LA \pi_{\rm LA} beats the EI stop by more than one increment’s cost: once the whole pool and horizon are in play, the EI stop is premature on average under the planning law, and the pre-registered statement that it is near-optimal at full scale is contradicted there. At the two highest costs π LA \pi_{\rm LA} gains less than one increment’s cost, as the reduced instances suggest, but no cell can be certified near-optimal, because the relaxation, and the term that carries it over to the planning law’s restriction to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , leave the upper bound loose. At low cost, then, lookahead over more arms and increments finds value under the planning law that two steps on three arms miss.

sections.heading: Calibration of the Gate.
sections.text: An open gate is a proof under the planning law: the certified lower bound where the gate first opens bounds the expected gain of continuing under the planning law. The recorded curves show how much of it arrives (Table 7 ). The realized gain falls below the certified lower bound on LCBench, with a band below zero, and exceeds it on PD1 and ODBench, with bands above zero. The means hide how the gains are spread: on every benchmark most departures lose on the recorded curve, and on PD1 and ODBench a minority of large gains carries the mean above the bound. On LCBench the planning law overstates what continuing is worth, which is where H2 stopping’s band falls below zero at the middle costs (Table 1 ). The certificate is sound under the planning law; what a departure earns depends on how well the planning law predicts the next increments. E.6 Sensitivity to the Surrogate’s Settings
sections.text: We rerun EI stopping under GP-atJ with one of its settings changed at a time: the fresh-observation noise variance (both its constant and its decaying term) scaled by 1 4 \frac{1}{4} or 4 4 , or both prior variances v a v_{a} and v t v_{t} scaled by 1 2 \frac{1}{2} or 2 2 . Pools, seeds, costs, caps and the stopping rule are unchanged, and each variant is paired per episode with the primary settings (Table 13 ). No change helps everywhere: each moves mean utility by up to 0.047 0.047 , in a direction, judged by band, that depends on the benchmark. Less fresh noise shortens episodes and helps on LCBench and PD1 but hurts on ODBench; more noise lengthens them, as a lower cost would, and hurts on LCBench and PD1 while helping on ODBench at most costs. When the arm with the largest EI lies below the incumbent, its EI grows with the predictive standard deviation, so cost and the surrogate’s scale are confounded: λ \lambda is the formulation’s single economic parameter, and the scale is a second one, fixed in advance. Halving the prior variances helps on LCBench and ODBench and is mixed on PD1. Choosing a setting on ODBench would compromise its held-out role. The same rescalings, and a noise variance calibrated per task from the recorded curves of the other tasks of its benchmark, were then applied to GP-at and GP-atJ together, paired per episode on seeds 1–50, to ask whether GP-atJ’s advantage under EI stopping depends on the surrogate’s scale (Table 14 ). At the primary settings GP-atJ has the higher mean utility in 19 of 21 cells, with bands above zero in 13 and below in 0. At the five other settings, in the order of the columns, the bands lie above zero in 9, 10, 15, 9 and 8 cells and below in 0, 0, 0, 1 and 1. The advantage thus survives every rescaling tried, with at most one band below zero. sections.heading: F.1 Comparators
sections.text: Every comparator runs on the pool and seed of the matched GP-atJ episode, reads the same fixed-table scores (Assumption 2 ) and is capped at B = 300 B=300 increments, following Lee et al. (2025) . A per-task rescaling by the extremes of the full curve tensor would reveal the task optimum; the utilities are therefore on our scale and do not transfer to the numbers published with CFBO. FT-PFN accepts training steps only as fractions of the curve length, and DyHPO’s deep-kernel GP divides every budget by the benchmark’s maximum; both are thus given each task’s native curve length, which our Gaussian surrogates never use. ifBO and DyHPO have no stopping rule ( Rakotoarison et al., 2024 ; Wistuba et al., 2022 ) and use all B B increments; their actions do not depend on λ \lambda , and one trajectory per task and seed thus gives the utility at all seven costs. For ifBO and CFBO-NT the first increment goes to a uniformly random configuration.

sections.heading: ifBO.
sections.text: ifBO ( Rakotoarison et al., 2024 ) scores each configuration by MFPI-random, the probability that its score after h h more steps exceeds f best + 10 − u ​ ( 1 − f best ) f_{\rm best}+10^{-u}(1-f_{\rm best}) , with h h uniform between one step and the curve length (capped by the remaining budget) and u ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 1 , 4 ) u\sim\mathcal{U}(1,4) redrawn at every step, and advances the selected configuration by one step. As in the code of Rakotoarison et al. (2024) , FT-PFN receives each configuration’s curve under its own identifier, numbered from one by first evaluation, and an unevaluated configuration is queried with identifier zero. A partially trained configuration keeps its identifier. Up to 100 unevaluated configurations are drawn per step, covering the whole 32-configuration pool. The budget is B = 300 B=300 , below the 1,000 steps of Rakotoarison et al. (2024) , since a 32-configuration pool cannot absorb them on any ODBench task or on two PD1 tasks.

sections.heading: CFBO-NT.
sections.text: The no-transfer baseline of Lee et al. (2025) , the only comparator with its own stopping rule, keeps CFBO’s acquisition, the expected utility improvement maximized over future increments, and its regret-based stopping rule with the published adaptive threshold ( 0.2 0.2 when the improvement probability is 1 / 2 1/2 , Beta-CDF shape e − 1 e^{-1} ). It uses FT-PFN in place of the full method’s transfer-trained extrapolator, and the public code’s context encoding, which gives no configuration its own identifier. sections.heading: DyHPO.
sections.text: DyHPO ( Wistuba et al., 2022 ) runs as released, through its own experiment loop. Its acquisition is EI at the next fidelity over the best score observed at that fidelity (or, if none, at lower fidelities), with no cost term, and it advances the selected configuration by one increment. Its deep-kernel GP is trained within each episode (10 restarts of 1,000 1{,}000 epochs, then 50 50 per increment), and its feature scaler is refit on each pool; it therefore sees pool-relative hyperparameter features where the other methods use fixed configuration arrays.

sections.heading: F.3 EI Stopping on DyHPO’s Surrogate
sections.text: Policy. The rule of Appendix F.2 runs on DyHPO’s deep-kernel GP, the released code with its feature extractor, scaler, training schedule, seeds and hyperparameters unchanged and retrained after every observation, on the comparator’s pools and seeds; the first increment is DyHPO’s initial design. EI is DyHPO’s closed-form Gaussian EI at each configuration’s next increment, taken over the best score observed so far, where DyHPO takes the best at that fidelity; the trajectory can therefore depart from DyHPO’s before any stop. Results (Tables 2 and 15 ). Relative to DyHPO run to B B , EI stopping reduces the score by 0.2 0.2 to 1.4 1.4 percentage points and saves 39 39 to 188 188 increments. The utility-difference band is above zero in every cell except the lowest PD1 cost, measuring how the chosen λ \lambda values the saved increments against the score reduction. EI stopping uses more increments on this surrogate than on FT-PFN in all but one cell; its utility-difference band relative to FT-PFN lies below zero in 18 of 21 cells.

sections.heading: F.4 Certificate Requirements for the Learned Surrogates
sections.text: The present certificate uses the affine Gaussian updates of Section 5 . The enclosure of Proposition 6 needs each child predictive to be a Gaussian restricted to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] whose mean is affine in the root observation and whose scale does not depend on it; FT-PFN’s child predictive is the network re-evaluated on each fantasized context, with no known form, so endpoint evaluations cannot enclose the integrand. DyHPO retrains after every observation, and its feature extractor also reads the observed curve; its refitted child predictors likewise fall outside this enclosure. The policy-improvement argument requires a fixed operational transition rule. Frozen FT-PFN weights define such a rule, as does a prescribed DyHPO retraining procedure with its random state included. Applying Proposition 1 requires evaluating those same updates at every fantasized child. Omitting the refit evaluates a different transition rule. Neither freezing weights nor specifying a retraining rule supplies the rigorous integrand bounds needed by our numerical gate.

sections.heading: The Gap between the Planning Law and the Curves.
sections.text: The formulation has no term for the distance between p θ p_{\theta} and the process behind the curves and no uncertainty over θ \theta . Our certified implementation fixes θ \theta in advance; incorporating learning into its transition rule would require enclosures for the resulting predictive updates. The guarantees transfer to real curves only as far as the planning law does, and the effect of λ \lambda depends on θ \theta (Appendix E.6 ).

sections.heading: A Payoff on the Best Noisy Reading.
sections.text: The incumbent is the best observed score, and the planning law adds fresh noise, so part of the value in ( 1 ) is the chance of a favorable reading. A deployed configuration is worth its held-out score, which the formulation conflates with the noisy score that selects it; when the surrogate’s noise exceeds the benchmark’s, the objective credits continuation with value the curves cannot deliver.

sections.heading: The Fidelity Unit and Other Simplifications.
sections.text: An action advances one benchmark-defined increment at cost λ \lambda , and the planning law is written in the same unit (its noise decay and basis scales are in checkpoints); the native horizon, the checkpoint spacing and the training behind a checkpoint appear in neither. The unit is one epoch on LCBench and ODBench and one retained checkpoint on PD1, so the same λ \lambda , lookahead depth and θ \theta mean different things across benchmarks, whose differences confound the tasks with how finely each records training. Paired comparisons within a task are unaffected; invariance to regridding is untested. Further, the cost is uniform, though real cost per epoch varies with the architecture; the pool is fixed; replay makes resumption free, records one realization of training noise per curve and caps curves that would continue; and allocation is sequential, where freeze–thaw BO systems often run parallel workers.

sections.heading: Extensions.
sections.text: A gate that opens only when the two-step lower bound is positive for every θ \theta in a box declared in advance would prove the stop premature under every θ \theta in the box; guaranteeing that continuing then improves on EI stopping under every θ \theta would also need a robust reference rule. A payoff on the posterior mean of the recommended configuration’s latent score would remove the value of favorable noisy readings, at the cost of rederiving ( 3 ) and the same-arm reduction. A learned surrogate trained on horizon-free inputs and then frozen would fall under Section 4 . Writing the planning law and λ \lambda on cumulative compute, as in cost-varying settings ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) , would give λ \lambda the same meaning on every grid; EI stopping would still look one grid step ahead, so whether its decisions survive regridding remains to be tested. Regret-bound and probabilistic-regret stopping ( Makarova et al., 2022 ; Wilson, 2024 ) with tolerance λ \lambda would be cost-aware rivals to EI stopping.

Long Vu Email: long-vu@outlook.com Jongseong Brad Choi Affiliation: State University of New York Korea Virginia Tech Stony Brook University Binoy Ravindran Zhoulai Fu Affiliation: State University of New York Korea Virginia Tech Stony Brook University Abstract Freeze–thaw Bayesian optimization (BO) evaluates candidates in resumable increments but usually stops at a budget or convergence test. We maximize a budget-free utility, the best observed score minus a cost per increment, with a one-step lookahead: advance the candidate with the largest expected improvement (EI) under a fixed surrogate, and stop once no EI exceeds the cost. This rule, EI stopping , never falls below stopping immediately in expected utility, yet it can stop too early. We construct a certificate, a lower bound on the value of two-step lookahead, that proves such a stop premature, and repeating this correction never lowers expected utility under the surrogate. Under the surrogate, EI stops are premature on average at low costs and lose little at high costs. On three hyperparameter optimization benchmarks, a pre-registered test finds EI stopping noninferior to the correction in most high-cost settings, while the correction gains at low costs on two of the three; more information sharing in the surrogate raises EI stopping’s utility. On the surrogates of two published methods, EI stopping trades lower scores for fewer training increments. EI stopping is a simple cost-aware reference whose utility depends on the surrogate. 1 Introduction Freeze–thaw Bayesian optimization (BO) allocates evaluation effort among candidates in resumable increments, allowing any candidate’s evaluation to be paused and resumed ( Swersky et al., 2014 ; Rakotoarison et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2025 ) . In hyperparameter optimization (HPO), candidates are hyperparameter configurations and increments are epochs or checkpoints. The original Freeze–Thaw BO method ( Swersky et al., 2014 ) and later learning-curve models use this to allocate training adaptively ( Wistuba et al., 2022 ; Kadra et al., 2023 ; Rakotoarison et al., 2024 ) , and curve extrapolation also ends unpromising runs early ( Domhan et al., 2015 ; Dai et al., 2019 ; Adriaensen et al., 2023 ) . These searches usually end at a supplied budget ( Swersky et al., 2014 ; Wistuba et al., 2022 ; Rakotoarison et al., 2024 ) , by a regret-based convergence test ( Makarova et al., 2022 ; Ishibashi et al., 2023 ; Wilson, 2024 ) or by a utility-regret threshold ( Lee et al., 2025 ) . We treat allocation and stopping in fixed-pool freeze–thaw BO as one decision problem and maximize the utility y ~ τ − λ ​ τ \tilde{y}_{\tau}-\lambda\tau , the best score observed when the search stops after τ \tau evaluation increments minus a cost λ \lambda per increment (Section 3.1 ). The cost alone governs termination, so no budget or horizon is needed, and maximizing utility minimizes the cost-adjusted simple regret of Xie et al. (2026) with a uniform cost (Appendix G ). We study a simple rule that targets this objective, EI stopping: train the configuration with the largest expected improvement (EI) ( Jones et al., 1998 ) while max i ⁡ EI i > λ \max_{i}\mathrm{EI}_{i}>\lambda and stop otherwise. EI-threshold stopping has been analyzed for its regret ( Nguyen et al., 2017 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) , and for complete evaluations Xie et al. (2026) derive the threshold from the Pandora’s box index ( Weitzman, 1979 ) . The rule looks one step ahead: the Bellman equation splits the value of an advance into its net gain EI i − λ \mathrm{EI}_{i}-\lambda and a nonnegative option value (Equation ( 3 )), and EI stops are Bellman-optimal under forward closure (Theorem 1 ), which learning curves need not satisfy: an unprofitable increment can unlock a later fidelity, or reveal which other configuration deserves training (Appendix A.4 ); the second requires a surrogate that shares information across configurations (Proposition 4 ). We ask whether EI stopping is limited by the depth of its lookahead or by the surrogate. We compare it, exactly under the surrogate and on recorded curves, with H2 stopping , its certified two-step correction, which keeps greedy EI allocation and at an EI stop certifies a candidate advance by its two-step continuation value. Our contributions are as follows. • Theory. We characterize premature EI stops through the Bellman option value and show that a positive lower bound on the value of a feasible two-step lookahead, the gate , proves an EI stop premature under the surrogate. The bound isolates a switching premium that arises only when the surrogate shares information across configurations, and repeating the gate at every EI stop never lowers expected utility, for any finite cap on further training (Section 4 ). EI stopping itself trains for at most 1 / λ 1/\lambda further increments in expectation and never falls below stopping immediately (Lemma 1 ), the freeze–thaw BO counterpart of the guarantee of Xie et al. (2026) . • Certified computation. For Gaussian surrogates with affine fantasy updates, slope-screened endpoint enclosures bound the selected configuration’s H2 advantage with directed rounding ( Fousse et al., 2007 ) (Section 4.3 ). • Controlled empirical study. We build three Gaussian learning-curve surrogates, GP-a, GP-at and GP-atJ, that share asymptotes across configurations and differ only in how they share transients: not at all, through the hyperparameter kernel, or also through a task-wide term; GP-atJ is the primary surrogate (Section 5 ). We cross them with EI stopping and H2 stopping on LCBench ( Zimmer et al., 2021 ) , PD1 ( Wang et al., 2024 ) and the held-out ODBench ( Lee et al., 2025 ) (Section 6 ). Four findings emerge. (F1) Under the surrogate, EI stops are premature on average at low costs and lose little at high costs. (F2) On recorded curves, certified departures gain most at low costs, except on LCBench, and little at high costs, where EI stopping is mostly noninferior. (F3) The pattern holds across all three Gaussian surrogates, and more information sharing significantly raises EI stopping’s average utility. (F4) On the surrogates of ifBO and DyHPO, EI stopping trades lower scores for fewer training increments. 2 Background and Related Work Learning-Curve Models and Sharing. Freeze–Thaw BO couples asymptotes through a GP over hyperparameters, models transients independently, and has no rule for ending the search ( Swersky et al., 2014 ) . DyHPO, DPL, LC-PFN and ifBO/FT-PFN are learned alternatives ( Wistuba et al., 2022 ; Kadra et al., 2023 ; Adriaensen et al., 2023 ; Rakotoarison et al., 2024 ) , and CFBO adds cost-sensitive acquisition, a stopping rule and a transfer-trained extrapolator ( Lee et al., 2025 ) . Our controls are Gaussian processes ( Rasmussen and Williams, 2006 ) that keep the asymptote-plus-transient form of Freeze–Thaw BO’s learning-curve model; they isolate information sharing while keeping fantasies certifiable. Cost-Aware Stopping. EI-threshold termination has prior treatments ( Nguyen et al., 2017 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . The closest work to our objective is Xie et al. (2026) , who pair a cost-aware stopping rule with PBGI and LogEIPC ( Xie et al., 2024 ) , the log variant ( Ament et al., 2023 ) of EI per unit cost ( Snoek et al., 2012 ) ; under uniform cost, LogEIPC with their rule is EI stopping. Their evaluations are complete, a full 51-epoch run on LCBench, and multi-fidelity evaluation is listed as an extension; we study freeze–thaw BO, where an action is one epoch or checkpoint, and ask what downstream value the EI stopping boundary misses there. Other whole-search criteria use error scales, regret gaps or probabilistic tolerances ( Makarova et al., 2022 ; Ishibashi et al., 2023 ; Wilson, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . These tests are cost-blind: the cost of continuing does not enter them, whereas EI stopping weighs the expected gain of the next increment against its cost. Fixed-schedule methods ( Jamieson and Talwalkar, 2016 ; Li et al., 2018 ; Falkner et al., 2018 ; Li et al., 2020 ) follow a preset schedule. We compare with neither. Forward closure makes one-step stopping optimal in classical monotone problems and on transition-closed sets of metalevel states ( Chow et al., 1971 ; Ferguson, 2008 ; Hay et al., 2012 ) ; Theorem 1 gives the version for our setting. At a fixed EI stop, increasing the cost cannot increase the optimal continuation premium. We compute the gap to the Bellman optimum exactly on small instances: EI stopping episodes under GP-atJ, frozen at their first EI stop and reduced to three arms with two further increments each ( 3 × 2 3{\times}2 instances) or two arms with three ( 2 × 3 2{\times}3 ; Appendix E.1 ). Dropping arms and increments only removes options, so the instances can show that a stop is premature but not that it is optimal in the full problem. On 840 pre-registered 3 × 2 3{\times}2 instances over all seven costs, the EI stop is exactly optimal in 72.5% and within one increment’s cost in 89.8%, and ideal H2 stopping, which uses the exact advantage, recovers 99.2% of the gap (85.5% on 2 × 3 2{\times}3 instances). The gap concentrates at low cost: at the two highest costs the stop is optimal in 84% and 78% of 3 × 2 3{\times}2 and 2 × 3 2{\times}3 instances, and below them in 68% and 54%. (Figure 1 ; Table 4 ).
